passages.title: Listen before joining others
passages.summary: Solomon’s opening teaches a learner to hear parents. Wisdom warns people against joining violent men. The men promise shared wealth. Their plan destroys lives, including their own.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me explains fearing God as love and obedience. Why does Wisdom warn that the violent men trap themselves?

passages.title: Search for wisdom
passages.summary: The teacher urges the learner to seek understanding. Wisdom guards against dishonest men and unfaithful partners. Learning requires listening and searching. The teacher connects understanding with fair actions toward others.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me invites readers to seek wisdom from God. Which actions does the teacher compare with searching for treasure?

passages.title: Trust God and help neighbors
passages.summary: The teacher urges trust in God, generous giving, and kind treatment of neighbors. Trust changes daily choices. The learner must give needed help without making a neighbor wait.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me teaches trust in the Lord. Why should the learner help a neighbor today rather than tomorrow?

passages.title: Choose a path carefully
passages.summary: A father recalls his own father’s teaching. He warns against joining people who harm others. The path image connects repeated choices with where a person’s life goes.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the path image with following the Lord. How do speech, sight, and steps affect the path the learner follows?

passages.title: Remain faithful to your wife
passages.summary: The teacher warns against adultery, sex that breaks marriage promises. He urges delight in one’s wife. The tempting invitation hides harm to health, work, and relationships.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What costs does the teacher describe beyond the first attraction?

passages.title: Promises, work, and harmful acts
passages.summary: The teacher warns about unpaid debts, laziness, lying, and adultery. He describes ants preparing food. Careless promises can put others’ debts on the learner. Planning and honest work reduce that danger.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does the ant’s work differ from the sleeper’s choices?

passages.title: A learner follows a tempting invitation
passages.summary: The teacher watches a young man meet a married woman. She persuades him to follow her. Her words hide the risk. The teacher compares his unthinking steps with animals approaching traps.
passages.uncertainty: Egypt names the cloth’s origin, not the scene’s location.

lds.text: Which details show the difference between her promises and the danger?

passages.title: Wisdom speaks in public
passages.summary: Wisdom calls people to listen. She describes fair rule and her presence before God formed the earth. The poem gives wisdom a woman’s voice. Her public invitation contrasts with chapter 7’s secret meeting.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me points to the rejection of evil in verse 13. How does Wisdom’s public invitation differ from the woman’s invitation in chapter 7?

passages.title: Two women invite the learner
passages.summary: Wisdom prepares a meal and invites learners. Folly offers stolen food while hiding death. Both invitations sound welcoming. The learner must examine what each woman offers and where it leads.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What does Folly hide that Wisdom openly explains?

passages.title: Words and work affect others
passages.summary: Sayings compare honest work with laziness, truthful words with lies, and care with hatred. Speech can protect neighbors or harm them. The sayings connect character with repeated daily actions.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does hatred stir up quarrels while love covers offenses?

passages.title: Honesty in trade and community
passages.summary: Sayings condemn false weights, gossip, and withholding grain. They praise fair trade and generous help. Dishonest trade harms buyers. Sharing food supports people whom the wealthy could otherwise exploit.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does withholding grain affect the people who need it?

passages.title: Correction, work, and careful speech
passages.summary: Sayings praise learning from correction, caring for animals, and speaking words that heal. Rash words can wound like a sword. Honest advice and kindness can help someone recover.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does the chapter compare rash speech with a sword?

passages.title: Choose teachers and companions
passages.summary: Sayings discuss patient work, delayed hope, good companions, and parents correcting children. The poor can lose productive fields through injustice. Poverty does not always result from laziness.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Scripture Helps applies the rod image to loving, consistent teaching. How does verse 23 challenge blaming every poor person for poverty?

passages.title: Look beyond first impressions
passages.summary: Sayings compare careful thought with quick anger. They describe hidden grief and mistreatment of poor people. A cheerful face can hide pain. Wealth and appearances do not show a person’s whole experience.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why should the learner look beyond laughter when judging someone’s happiness?

passages.title: Answer gently and accept advice
passages.summary: Sayings praise gentle answers, careful listening, and loving homes. They warn against anger and greed. A gentle answer can reduce anger. A loving meal matters more than expensive food with hatred.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me teaches kind words and patient answers. How do gentle words change the direction of a quarrel?

passages.title: Plans need humility and self-control
passages.summary: Sayings discuss God weighing motives, rulers judging fairly, and pride preceding a fall. Winning a city requires force. Controlling anger requires strength directed at one’s own actions.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me applies these sayings to how people communicate. Why does the chapter value controlling anger above capturing a city?

passages.title: Peace, friendship, and fair judgment
passages.summary: Sayings praise quiet homes and lasting friends. They warn against gossip, bribery, and unfair judgments. Repeated gossip can separate friends. A judge who accepts payment harms people seeking a fair hearing.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How do repeated accusations damage a friendship?

passages.title: Listen before answering
passages.summary: Sayings warn against answering too soon. They describe arguments, unreliable wealth, and a faithful friend. The first account can sound convincing. Hearing questions and the other person can reveal missing facts.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why should a judge hear more than the first person’s account?

passages.title: Wealth changes how people treat neighbors
passages.summary: Sayings describe friends abandoning poor people. They praise patience, generosity, and teaching children. People may seek a wealthy friend’s gifts rather than friendship. Helping the poor serves God.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does the chapter expose friendships that depend on wealth?

passages.title: Trade honestly and avoid revenge
passages.summary: Sayings warn about wine, false weights, careless promises, and paying back harm. A buyer pretends goods have little value, then boasts. His words serve his own advantage.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What does the buyer’s changed story reveal about his honesty?

passages.title: Justice matters more than offerings
passages.summary: Sayings discuss fair conduct, dishonest wealth, ignored cries, and plans for battle. Religious gifts do not excuse harmful actions. Refusing to hear the poor can leave others without help.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does the chapter place fair conduct above an offering?

passages.title: A good name and fair treatment
passages.summary: Sayings compare a good name with riches. A new teaching section warns against robbing poor people. Rich and poor share one maker. A person’s wealth does not justify taking advantage of them.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Scripture Helps teaches loving correction and rejects using the rod to justify abuse. Why does the teacher mention God when forbidding harm to poor people?

passages.title: Control appetite and protect others’ property
passages.summary: The teacher warns about deceptive hosts, chasing wealth, taking land, and repeated drunkenness. Moving a boundary steals land. Children without a protecting father face particular danger from powerful neighbors. McClellan reads the rod sayings as physical punishment.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does the teacher warn against entering the fields of fatherless children?

passages.title: Rescue people and examine your work
passages.summary: The teacher urges rescue of people facing death. He warns against delighting in an enemy’s fall. Claiming ignorance does not remove responsibility to help. An enemy’s suffering does not justify celebration.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What excuse does the teacher reject when someone needs rescue?

passages.title: Hezekiah’s men collect Solomon’s sayings
passages.summary: Hezekiah’s men copy sayings about rulers, disputes, friendship, and helping enemies. Offering food to an enemy changes the response to conflict. Revenge need not decide the next action.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What does feeding a hungry enemy require beyond winning an argument?

passages.title: Choose when to answer foolish speech
passages.summary: Sayings warn both against answering a fool and against leaving foolish claims unanswered. The paired warnings require judgment. An answer can either repeat the foolishness or challenge false confidence.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How can the two warnings in verses 4–5 fit different situations?

passages.title: Care for friends and flocks
passages.summary: Sayings praise honest friends and nearby help. They urge careful attention to sheep and goats. Wealth does not last forever. Knowing the flock’s condition supports food and clothing for the household.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does the teacher connect daily care for animals with the household’s future?

passages.title: Honest poverty and harmful wealth
passages.summary: Sayings compare honest poor people with crooked rich people. They condemn rulers who exploit the weak. Having little does not make someone less honest. Wealth can hide harm, including profits from unfair loans.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Which actions show that a wealthy person has harmed poorer neighbors?

passages.title: Rulers, anger, and teaching children
passages.summary: Sayings connect fair rulers with public joy. They warn against bribery, uncontrolled anger, and neglected children. A ruler’s choices affect many households. Listening to poor people helps protect fair judgment.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does hearing a poor person’s case affect a ruler’s work?

passages.title: Agur asks for enough
passages.summary: Agur admits limited understanding. He asks for enough food and describes lessons from animals. He fears that riches could lead him to forget God. Hunger could lead him to steal.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does Agur ask for neither poverty nor riches?

passages.title: A mother advises a king
passages.summary: Lemuel recalls his mother’s warning about drink and unfair judgment. A poem praises a capable woman. The woman buys land, makes goods, feeds her household, and helps the poor. Her work benefits others.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me praises the woman’s strength, skill, and influence. How do the woman’s business decisions help both her household and poor neighbors?
